issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette: Dr. Ricardo Alvarez, a 70-year-old widowed dentist who had emigrated from Cuba as a young man, had built a quiet, orderly life in Miami. That order was shattered on a Tuesday morning seven months ago, when a car bomb detonated outside a community center he was passing. The blast threw him against a parked van. He remembers the pressure wave, the acrid smoke, the ringing silence afterward, and the sight of a man in a blue uniform-a security guard-lying motionless nearby, his face obscured by debris. In the months since, Ricardo had come to believe that he should have seen it coming, that his failure to notice the abandoned vehicle was a personal failing. He repeatedly blamed himself for not warning anyone, a rumination that circled back on itself each night. This self-blame was a quiet but constant companion, and it was one reason he now carried a small, unlicensed revolver in his medical bag-a decision that felt less like a choice and more like a necessity. He had also stopped watching the news entirely, because any report about a bombing or political violence would send him into a spiral. The memories themselves were not like normal memories. When they returned, they felt completely real across all his senses at once-the heat of the blast, the smell of burnt rubber, the sight of the guard's uniform. He could not seem to put the event into words; when he tried, the emotion would overwhelm him so completely that he had to stop speaking, his hands trembling. These episodes were triggered most powerfully by gunshot noises-a car backfiring, a kid's firecracker-but also by simply seeing a person in uniform or overhearing someone discuss military topics. He had noticed that the more he tried to push the memory away, the more easily it resurfaced: a passing police cruiser, a veteran's cap in a grocery line, and suddenly he was back on that sidewalk. His vigilance had become exhausting. He watched other people closely for signs they might harm him, scanning their hands and faces as they entered his dental office, and he scanned for exits as soon as he entered any room or building. He was on high alert whenever he heard unexpected or loud sounds-a dropped tray, a slammed door-and his body would lock up before his mind even registered the noise. This constant threat monitoring made him irritable with patients, and he had started avoiding certain streets and public gatherings altogether. The causal loop was tight and self-reinforcing: a trigger like a police siren would spike his threat response, which would push him to check his weapon or avoid the news, which in turn made the memory more intrusive the next time he was startled. He had lost two long-time patients who complained he seemed "jumpy" and distracted. What finally brought Ricardo to seek help was a moment in his own waiting room. A new patient, a retired Army officer, was discussing a documentary about Middle Eastern conflicts with his wife. Ricardo froze mid-step, his hand on the door, the memory flooding back with full sensory force. He excused himself, locked his office, and sat in the dark for twenty minutes. That evening, he told his daughter he was afraid he was losing his mind. What frightened him most was the possibility that he would never feel safe again in his own city, in his own clinic-that the man in the blue uniform would follow him forever.
